title: Chapter 99 – Bench Fabrication
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Seven weeks later.

He earns the last point of the sixty on the morning of the forty-ninth day, from a patch of clover growing in the crack of a paving stone.

It is a poor way to finish a grind. The clover is small, three leaves on a hair-thin stem, the sort of thing nobody would notice or miss. He kneels on the cold slab outside his cell, with the dew soaking through his leggings, and lays his left palm against the green. The Spring Vein flares along his arm. The leaves go gray, then brown, then curl to dust under his hand. The living thing is gone, and what it was has gone into him as a faint cool sweetness, and into the panel as a number.

```
SPRING VEIN — DRAW
Source: clover (3 leaves). Consumed.
Yield: 1 CE.
CE: 60.
```

Sixty. He looks at the figure for a long time.

It has cost him seven weeks. Seven weeks of labor in the Pill Hall at two points a night and a cap of six a week, of draws at dawn from whatever small green life the thaw had pushed up, of tasks the Interface had logged in its flat way: a lesson taught, a tonic mixed, a page of the Founder's script translated for Elder Ye, an hour spent mending the Library's cracked door-hinge for a point and a half. Fifty-three, spent forty on a blank. Thirteen, grown back to sixty by inches. He has not bought a single plum. He has not read a single novel. He has seen his own face in the water bowl each morning and noticed it growing thinner.

Every advantage has a cost, he thinks. This one costs time, and time is the one thing I cannot print.

He wipes the dust from his hand. The panel waits.

* * *

Elder Ye signs his pass without reading it.

"Two hours," she says, in the herbal room, with her eyes on a scroll. A dozen girls from the Sutra Hall school are bent over the long tables behind her, drawing leaves. At the end of the row, Yue lifts her head, catches his eye, and goes carefully back to her slate. "I will tell Elder Qin that you are checking the bench's state. It is true."

"It is true."

"You have an unusual look."

"I have been counting a number for seven weeks."

"Ah." Ye dips her brush. "I find that the best use of a number is to spend it. Go."

He goes.

The Dock is as he left it. The hum, the pale light, the long stair of black stone that no longer smells of danger. He comes down it quickly. The bench waits at the bottom with its recess and its silver clamps and its gray hood, and for the first time in his life he looks at it without dread. He knows this machine now. It has measured him and sent a message to a stranger, and it has taught him a lesson in stillness that he is still learning. It has never once lied.

He does not lie down. He stands at the head of the bench and lays his hand flat on the cold metal.

"Operator Level 1," he says, quietly, in the Founder's script, which comes more easily now. "Request: Interface upgrade to Level 4. Bench synthesis."

The panel opens.

```
INTERFACE UPGRADE — LEVEL 4: BENCH SYNTHESIS
Requirement: Operator session completed ... MET.
Requirement: Dock 2 link ... ACTIVE.
Cost: 60 CE.
Effect: unlocks compound fabrication at ARK-6 bench.
- Combine up to 3 input materials into 1 output.
- Reference volumes accepted (see: Hundred Veins Forge, vol. 1).
- Output quality scales with input quality and CE spent.
- Fabrication is not free: each print costs CE.
Note: Level 4 is permanent. CE spent is not refunded.
Proceed? (60 CE)
```

Permanent. He reads the word twice. It is the only mercy on the panel.

He says yes.

The bench shudders. A line of cold blue light runs from the head of the recess to the foot, and the hood rises on its arm, and every silver clamp lifts and falls with a faint click, like a row of teeth. In his chest the Seal gives one long gold pulse. And in the corner of his eye the number falls, 60, 40, 20, 5, 0, and lies there, quiet.

```
UPGRADE COMPLETE.
Interface Level: 4.
New function: BENCH SYNTHESIS (compound fabrication).
CE: 0.
```

He stands in the humming dark, empty-handed. There is no flash, no vision, no sense of power. He feels exactly as he felt a moment ago. It is a curious thing, he reflects, to buy the right to spend more.

Then he goes back up the stair to begin again.

* * *

Ye is waiting for him in the herbal room when he comes up from the unlock.

The school has gone home. The long tables are bare, and the lamps are out, except one. She sits under it with her hands folded and a pot of tea going cold, as a woman sits who has been waiting a long time and does not wish it noticed.

"You are gray," she says.

"I have been told."

"You have bought something."

"A function." He sits, slowly. "I can make small things, now. At the bench. From things I bring. It costs a great deal."

"What kind of things?"

"Tools. Components. The first I mean to make is a plate, for Hu." He chooses his words with care. "It is a piece of the Veiled Forge. It is not the whole. It will let a refiner work where no Qi-reader can see."

Ye does not move. Behind her spectacles, in the lamplight, her eyes are very bright.

"The Veiled Forge," she says. "The lost craft of the Coral Gate."

"A portion."

"A portion." She exhales slowly. "Forty years, I have read about it. I have copied its legend into three books. I have sat in this room and imagined what it would be to find a single scrap." She looks at him. "And you mean to make one before the month is out."

"With a book that Hu brought. And a bench that has been waiting."

"You are very careful with your credit."

"It is not mine." He holds her gaze. "It belongs to the one who keeps the book. That is a refiner in my clan. I only carry."

A very faint smile touches her mouth. "You have a talent, Lin Jian, for being modest in a way that tells me exactly how proud you are."

She lifts the pot and pours him a cup of cold tea, and he drinks it, and for a minute neither of them says anything.

"There is a cost," she says finally.

"There is always a cost."

"Name it to me. Now. So I do not learn it from the Registry."

He draws a breath. "The bench takes CE. A kind of energy I earn by labor. It takes it by the dozen, and it takes it slowly. It will be weeks before I can make anything else. Months, if I want to make anything large." He pauses. "And each print strains the Seal."

"Strains it."

"A little. It heals. But it is not a thing I can do every day."

Ye nods slowly, as though that were exactly the answer she wanted.

"Then do it sparingly," she says. "And tell me before you do it. I would rather be your accomplice than your surprise."

* * *

The second grind is shorter, because he knows now what he is grinding for.

Four weeks, this time. The same labor, the same draws, the same careful accounting of every point. He eats little and sleeps late and does not ask the Sutra Hall for favors. Once Shen Yuhang passes him in the colonnade with two other Silver Leaf disciples, and stops, and says pleasantly, "You look exhausted, Gate Bearer. Do the Elders work you hard?" Jian answers that they do. Shen smiles, and walks on.

On the twenty-ninth day he stands at the bench with thirty CE in the bank.

He has laid out his materials on the shelf of the fabricator, the way the panel asked: three inputs, no more. The rule is strange to him, and he has turned it over for weeks. A recipe is a form of honesty. A machine that will not accept a fourth ingredient is a machine that has no patience for waste. The first is Old Hu's book, open to the diagram of the veins. The second is a bar of Pool-grade steel, wrapped in oilcloth, that has lain in a cupboard in the Garden's forge since the night the Blood Shadow Mu died. It is a span of dull gray metal, the heart of a blade that once cut a man in two. Hu cut it away from the ruined hilt with a hacksaw and a month of swearing, and sent it up the mountain in a crate with a note that said only: Use it before it makes me nervous.

The third is a thread of his own hair.

He looks at the strand lying across the metal, absurdly small. The panel had asked for a "personal reference," and he had considered, for a while, and decided that hair was the cheapest honest answer.

```
FABRICATION — PROPOSAL
Inputs:
1. Reference: Hundred Veins Forge, vol. 1 (coupling sequence, partial).
2. Base: Pool-grade steel bar (1; 340 g).
3. Personal: hair (1 strand, Operator).
Output (projected): COUPLING PLATE, "QUIET FIRE," grade: Pool-compatible.
Function: when set in a forge hearth, suppresses Qi and heat signature of the
forge and its work within 20 paces. Not an array. Cannot be sensed by a
Qi-reader below Core.
Cost: 30 CE.
CE: 30.
Proceed?
```

His mouth has gone dry.

Thirty. All I have. He thinks of the Seal, strained twice. He thinks of the soul vessel, still at eighty-three, and the forty points he owes it. He thinks of the old man waiting for his hammer. If he spends the thirty on the plate, the soul repair is another seven weeks away. If he spends it on the soul, the plate is another seven weeks away. And he does not have fourteen weeks.

The Court inspects the Garden every season. The Registry is writing to my mother. A clan that cannot arm itself is a clan that will be taken.

"Proceed," he says.

* * *

The bench takes seventy-one breaths to print the plate.

He counts them. The recess fills with a pale cold glare, and the steel bar goes first, melting into a pool, then a ribbon, then a lattice of threads that cross and weave in the air. The book's diagram is projected over it in white lines. His hair is consumed in a single blue flash. When the light fades, a small plate lies on the shelf: dark gray, the size of his palm, etched on one face with the same fine regular pattern as the blank, but deeper. More alive.

He lifts it. It is warm.

```
FABRICATION COMPLETE.
Item: Coupling Plate, "Quiet Fire."
Quality: Good (Pool-compatible).
Note: use requires a forge master with the Hundred Veins coupling sequence.
CE: 0.
```

Good. Not perfect. But he holds in his hand the first piece of a craft that has been dead for six hundred years, and Hu's book lies open beside it with a diagram of the veins that is, at last, no longer a riddle.

Pebble sniffs the plate and sneezes.

Quiet, it says. Very. Like nothing.

"That is what it is for."

Nothing is nice, says Pebble, with great seriousness. But not all the time.

He wraps the plate in a clean cloth, tucks it inside his tunic, and goes up the stair to wait for the new moon.

* * *

The Garden at night in the fourth month is the best place in the world.

He has not been home for eight weeks. The pass is signed, the moon is down, and he walks the last mile on foot from the town road in the dark, with Pebble on his shoulder and the plate against his ribs. The cold has gone. The air is wet and sweet. There are frogs in the irrigation ditches, and a nightingale somewhere in the pines, and when he comes round the last bend the whole of Green Pine Garden lies below him, a long low sprawl of sheds and terraces and tiled roofs, with lamps burning in a dozen windows.

It is bigger than he remembers. Two new rooftops stand beyond the granary. A fence runs along the east boundary where none stood before. In the yard behind the forge a torch is burning and a line of figures is moving through a drill in the dark: staves up, step, strike, step. Hu's guards. They number twenty now, and the new ones are very young.

His mother meets him at the gate.

She does not run. She does not weep. She stands with her hands folded in front of her, in the lamplight, thinner than he remembers, with a streak of white in her hair that was not there at the Mountain Gate. She looks at him for a long, searching minute, and he realizes that she is counting him: ribs, shoulders, color. Then her mouth softens.

"You are better," she says.

"I am fed."

"You are fed. It is not the same." She takes his face in both hands, briefly, and lets go. "Your father is in the forge with Hu. He has been there since sunset. They will not tell me what for. I know that you are bringing something."

"I will tell you all of it."

"After you eat." Her voice is brisk, but there is a catch in it. "There is soup. And your sister-in-law's pie."

"I have no sister-in-law."

"You do not," says Qinghe serenely. "But Feng has been very attentive to the Tan niece, and I am keeping the pie in case."

He laughs. It surprises him, a bright short sound in the dark, and she smiles back, and for a moment they stand in the lamplight like two people who have forgotten the rest of the world.

Then they go in.

* * *

Wenyuan finds him in the study at midnight, bent over the ledger by a single lamp.

It is the small room off the main hall where the Patriarch keeps the Garden's accounts, a room that smells of ink and old rice paper. Shelves line the walls. A map of the clan's lands is pinned above the desk, with seventy-one small paper tags clustered along the east terraces, each tag a name. Jian has been reading the figures for an hour. They are better than he expected, and they frighten him a little.

"You should be asleep," says his father.

"I could say the same."

"I am the Patriarch. Insomnia is in the contract." Wenyuan lowers himself into the chair opposite and rubs his eyes. "I was thinking of the Garden Hall."

"The Hall?"

"The council has a proposal. Seventy-one people cannot be run from a kitchen table. We need a house. A real one, with a roll, a treasury, a seat in the town. The Court trust forbids new structures inside the Garden. But there is a plot at the foot of the hill, by the road, that belongs to no one." He pushes a folded paper across the desk. "A deed. It is cheap. It is cheap because it floods every spring."

Jian opens it. The ground is a narrow strip of low meadow, fifty paces by two hundred, along the river road.

"It will flood."

"It will flood, and the Court will not mind, because a clan house in the town is a thing they can see. It will cost four hundred stones for the timber, two hundred for the labor." Wenyuan smiles faintly. "I do not have six hundred stones."

"I do not either."

"I know. I am not asking." He rubs his thumb along the edge of the desk. "I want you to know it is there. A clan that is only a Garden is a hiding place. A clan with a house is a family. We have been hiding for a long time, Jian. I think it is time to stop."

Jian looks at the deed for a while. At the careful hand, the blotted seal, the ink still faintly wet.

"We will build it," he says. "Not this year. But we will."

"I believe you," says Wenyuan. "That is the strange thing. I used to think you were a very odd boy. I am not sure I knew you. I am not sure I know you now." He pauses. "But I believe you."

* * *

The Veiled Forge is not a place. It is a state of mind.

That is how Hu puts it, hours later, in the forge shed, with the shutters closed and the door barred and a bar of dull gray steel glowing in the hearth. His one hand is on the tongs. His face is lit orange by the fire. His eyes are fixed on the coupling plate, which lies in the coals at the heart of the hearth like a piece of black ice, and on the diagram propped against the anvil, and he is not speaking to anyone in particular.

"The Forge is a place where a thing is made to agree with itself," he recites, low. "Hammer and metal and Qi are three voices. The master teaches them to sing a single note."

Wenyuan stands by the door with his arms folded, watching. Feng sits on an upturned bucket. Jian leans against the wall with his hand on the plate's cloth, ready, though he does not know for what.

"Lower the fire," Hu says.

Feng pumps the bellows once, softly. The glow dims.

"Lower."

Another stroke. The coals go from orange to red to a deep dull ruby, almost black. The heat in the shed does not fall. It quiets. Jian feels it settle, as a hush settles over a crowd, and the sounds of the Garden outside, the frogs, the drilling guards, the nightingale, fade away as if a door had closed on them.

"There," says Hu, very softly. "There it is."

He lifts the bar from the coals with the tongs, and sets it on the anvil, and picks up his hammer.

The first blow does not ring.

It falls on the steel with a soft deep thud, like a hand on a drum, and the bar flattens a finger's width. The second blow is the same. The third. The old man works in a kind of trance, his shoulders loose, his breath slow, his whole body moving as one with the hammer, and the steel answers. It darkens as it cools. Fine lines of silver crawl up its flanks like veins. Every time the hammer falls, the lines brighten a little, and run, and join.

The veins in the metal, Jian thinks. The lines of Qi in the work. Brought into one.

He has watched Hu work a hundred times. He has never seen this. It is not skill, quite. It is a kind of listening.

The bar becomes a blade. The blade becomes three, short and straight, a hand's breadth longer than a dagger, a shade darker than the steel they were cut from. Hu quenches the first in a trough of black oil. There is no hiss, no steam. The oil simply takes the heat and gives nothing back.

He lifts it. Turns it in the light of the dimmed coals.

And the old man's face crumples.

"Hu," says Wenyuan, taking a step.

"No, leave it." The old refiner's voice is rough. He holds the blade up to the fire. "It is good. It is very good. It is the best thing I have ever made." His one hand has begun to shake, and the blade with it. "I made a forge in the quiet. Thirty years I waited. Thirty years, and I did it in an hour, in a shed behind a Garden, with a boy's plate and a dead man's steel."

"It was the book, Hu," Jian says gently. "And the hand."

"It was the boy." Hu wipes his eyes with the back of his wrist, and leaves a streak of soot across his cheek. "Do not argue. I know what I know."

He lays the blade on the anvil with great care. Then he sits down on the floor with his back against the hearth, and weeps, silently, without shame, and nobody in the shed speaks for a long time.

* * *

The cost arrives in the morning. It always does. The Interface never charges at the till; it sends the bill by a later hand.

He feels it first as a weakness, a thin gray fatigue behind the eyes. He has not slept. He has spent the night watching the old man work, and then helping to carry the three blades to the wall, and drinking his mother's soup. At dawn, in the cold yard, he lays a hand on the well-curb, and finds that his legs have gone.

Thirty CE, he thinks. The Seal strained, from the plate's coupling. A night without sleep.

"Brother." Feng's hand under his arm. "You are gray."

"I am tired."

"You are more than tired." His brother's voice is low. "Hu says the blades are quiet. He says no sensor in the Sect will find them. But he says there is another thing." Feng pauses. "He says the shed is quiet too."

Jian lifts his head.

"The forge was veiled while it ran. The Quiet Fire reaches twenty paces. It swallowed every sound, every flicker of Qi. Inside the circle, Hu says, it was like standing in a hole in the world." His brother's jaw tightens. "But a hole in the world is still a hole. If someone were watching the Garden from the ridge..."

He does not need to finish.

The Court's array on the Mountain Gate, Jian thinks slowly. The Sect's sensors on the north slope. A Garden that has hummed with Qi every night for a year, and then, for four hours, does not.

He turns. Behind the granary, on the road from the town, a thin line of dust is rising in the gray dawn. A sedan chair, black lacquer, with a gilded roof and the Court's silver crest on the door. Four porters, moving fast.

And behind it, riding in single file on gray horses, six Enforcement officers in the silver-and-black of the Registry's escort.

"Inspector Dai," says Feng.

"Early," says Jian.

"The blades," says Feng, low.

"Where?"

"On the wall of the forge. In plain sight. Hu said they were too good to hide."

"Then we do not hide them." Jian pushes himself off the well-curb. His legs hold, barely. "Tell Hu to take them down and rub them with ash. They are old stock, cut from a ruined sword the clan has kept for years. That is true. Say nothing of the plate."

"And the hole in the world?"

"A flue fell in. A chimney fire. Hu cursed it for three hours and put it out with sand." He meets his brother's eyes. "It is the sort of story a Court inspector believes, because it is dull."

Feng nods once, and goes at a run.

Jian stays where he is. He wipes the sweat from his face, and straightens his cloak, and puts on the expression of a quiet young man who has come home for a visit and slept badly. He has about four minutes. It will have to be enough.

The chair comes on down the hill. In the yard behind him, the guards have stopped drilling, and are standing very still.
